Shields (University of Toledo), 'Information Theory and Statistics: A Tutorial', Foundations and Trends in Communications and Information Theory, Vol. 1, No. 4 (2004), pp. 417-528, now Publishers Inc. The local file is the publisher PDF held in books-d-models under the filename 'Csiszar & Shields (2004) - Information Theory and Statistics - A Tutorial.pdf'; the catalog filename given in the assignment (CsiszarShields-2004-FoundationsAndTrendsInfoTheory.pdf) does not exist on disk. File size 730,600 bytes; sha256 over (str(size) encoded + full file bytes) = 995225b57e1135c6119606508dad0fbeb16d56f2a0f2669c17c659c4e7c1aeae; book_id is the first 16 hex characters. The extracted text (245,277 bytes) is complete for all eight sections and the appendix; extraction quirks: the divergence separator glyph renders as a control character, hats render as combining circumflex accents, and the not-equal sign in the appendix renders as an equals sign, so verbatim quotes were drawn from passages free of the corrupted glyphs. Motif-lane extraction (MOTIF-TIERB-DRAIN-01) of the same work for sync-cloud reconciliation.

primitives.name: Entropy of a distribution: expected surprise, in bits
primitives.verbatim_quote: The entropy H(P ) of a probability distribution P = {P (a), a ∈ A} is defined by the formula
primitives.latex: H(P) = -\sum_{a \in A} P(a) \log P(a)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(a): probability of symbol a, dimensionless, sums to 1 over A
symbol_and_unit_ledger.log: base 2 logarithm, so H(P) is in bits

assumptions: Finite alphabet A
Base two logarithms throughout the tutorial
primitives.breakdown_regime: Finite alphabet only; continuous alphabets need differential entropy, which can be negative and lacks the counting interpretation.

layer2.mapping: Entropy is the engine's baseline uncertainty meter for any categorical projection: a projected distribution over discrete outcomes carries H(P) bits of irreducible uncertainty, against which every signal's information gain is measured as an entropy reduction.
layer2.telemetry: Projected outcome distributions and realized outcome frequencies from settled events.

primitives.name: Information divergence (Kullback-Leibler distance): definition, nonnegative, zero only at equality (via the log-sum inequality)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The information measure known as information divergence or Kullback-Leibler distance or relative entropy plays a key role, often with a geometric flavor as an analogue of squared Euclidean distance
primitives.latex: D(P\|Q) = \sum_{a \in A} P(a) \log \frac{P(a)}{Q(a)}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(a), Q(a): probabilities of symbol a under the two distributions, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.D(P||Q): divergence in bits; +infinity if P(a) > 0 = Q(a) for some a
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p log(p/0): defined as +infinity, p log 0 conventions as in the source

assumptions: Log-sum inequality gives D(P||Q) >= 0 with equality iff P = Q
D is lower semi-continuous in (P, Q), continuous where Q is strictly positive
primitives.breakdown_regime: Asymmetric and no triangle inequality: it is a squared-distance analogue, not a metric. Infinite whenever the second argument excludes an event the first allows.

layer2.mapping: Divergence is the engine's universal scoring geometry: forecast versus realized distributions, prior versus updated beliefs, and model versus data are all compared in bits, and the score decomposes along projections instead of being a single opaque number.
layer2.telemetry: Any pair of categorical distributions the engine holds: projections, empirical frequencies, fused signal summaries.

primitives.name: Kraft inequality: a length function is a prefix code length function iff the dyadic sum is at most 1
primitives.verbatim_quote: A function L: A → N is the length function of some prefix code if and only if it satisfies the so-called Kraft inequality
primitives.latex: \sum_{a \in A} 2^{-L(a)} \le 1

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L(a): codeword length for symbol a, in bits (natural number)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.2^{-L(a)}: dyadic interval length claimed by codeword a, dimensionless

assumptions: Binary image alphabet
Prefix (instantaneously decodable) codes
primitives.breakdown_regime: Non-prefix codes beat the bound only by an additive log log |A| term (Theorem 1.2); the characterization is exact only for prefix codes.

layer2.mapping: The Kraft sum is a budget constraint the engine can reuse anywhere it allocates a finite resource over discrete alternatives: any set of nonnegative weights 2^{-L} summing to at most 1 is a valid code, hence a valid prior skeleton for a countable model list.
layer2.telemetry: Model lists with assigned code lengths, for example candidate model classes indexed by integers.

primitives.name: Shannon's noiseless coding theorem: expected prefix code length is at least the entropy, and the Shannon code beats entropy plus 1
primitives.verbatim_quote: A key consequence of the lemma is Shannon's noiseless coding theorem.
primitives.latex: H(P) \le E(L) < H(P) + 1 \quad \text{for the Shannon code } L(a) = \lceil -\log P(a) \rceil

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E(L): expected codeword length under P, bits per symbol
symbol_and_unit_ledger.H(P): entropy of the source distribution, bits

assumptions: Prefix codes
Known source distribution P
primitives.breakdown_regime: The plus 1 slack is per message for block codes it amortizes; with unknown P the bound is unattainable and redundancy (Sections 6-8) is the price.

layer2.mapping: This is the engine's achievability template: an ideal score (-log P of the realized outcome) plus a bounded rounding loss. Any internal scoring rule that claims to beat the entropy floor by more than the rounding slack is mis-specified.
layer2.telemetry: Realized outcomes scored under projected distributions; per-event log scores.

primitives.name: Arithmetic coding: interval subdivision by conditional probabilities gives practical prefix codes within 1 bit of Shannon codes
primitives.verbatim_quote: We close this introduction with a discussion of arithmetic codes, which are of both practical and conceptual importance.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Q_n: the coding process's marginal distribution on length n blocks
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L'(x_1^n): length of the second-kind arithmetic codeword, bits
symbol_and_unit_ledger.J(x_1^n): nested subinterval of [0,1) of length Q_n(x_1^n)

assumptions: Consistent marginals Q_n (they must come from a process)
Conditional probabilities Q(a | past) cheap to compute
primitives.breakdown_regime: First-kind arithmetic codes are one-to-one but not prefix; strict Shannon codes may be computationally prohibitive for large n, which is the gap arithmetic coding fills.

layer2.mapping: Arithmetic coding is sequential probability assignment made literal: the engine's running conditional probabilities ARE a code, so calibration of sequential forecasts and compression quality are the same measurement, and the plus 1 bit bound prices the conversion.
layer2.telemetry: Sequential conditional probability streams for ordered events.

primitives.name: Method of types: polynomially many empirical distributions, type class size about 2^{nH}, type class probability about 2^{-nD}
primitives.verbatim_quote: An important application of information theory is to the theory of large deviations. A key to this application is the theory of types.
primitives.latex: \frac{2^{nH(P)}}{\binom{n+|A|-1}{|A|-1}} \le |T_P^n| \le 2^{nH(P)}, \qquad P^n(T_Q^n) \doteq 2^{-nD(Q\|P)}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.T_P^n: type class: all length n sequences with empirical distribution P
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n-type: a distribution realizable as an empirical distribution at sample size n

assumptions: I.i.d. sampling from a fixed distribution on a finite alphabet
Polynomial factors are negligible on the exponential scale
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exponential approximations only: at small n the polynomial factors matter, and the method is tied to i.i.d. sampling on finite alphabets.

layer2.mapping: Types give the engine a counting-based evidence calculus: the probability of any empirical pattern is read off from its divergence to the assumed distribution, with no simulation, which is the fast path for tail questions about categorical count data.
layer2.telemetry: Count vectors and empirical distributions over finite outcome sets, with sample sizes.

primitives.name: Sanov's theorem: the probability that the empirical distribution falls in a set Pi decays with exponent D(Pi||P), the divergence to the nearest member
primitives.verbatim_quote: The empirical distribution P̂n in the Corollary converges to P with probability 1 as n → ∞, by the law of large numbers, or by the very Corollary (and Borel–Cantelli).
primitives.latex: -\frac{1}{n} \log \mathrm{Prob}(\hat P_n \in \Pi) \to D(\Pi\|P) = \inf_{Q \in \Pi} D(Q\|P)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Pi: a set of distributions, closure equal to closure of its interior
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P: the true, strictly positive sampling distribution
symbol_and_unit_ledger.D(Pi||P): infimum divergence from the set to the truth, bits

assumptions: Strictly positive true distribution
Regularity of Pi (closure equals closure of interior)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Only the exponent is identified, not the prefactor; sets touching the truth have exponent 0 and polynomial, not exponential, rarity.

layer2.mapping: Sanov is the engine's rare-pattern pricing rule: the plausibility of an observed empirical pattern under a working model is governed by the single nearest alternative distribution in the pattern's set, so stress questions reduce to one divergence minimization.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical distributions from samples; candidate pattern sets defined by moment or frequency constraints.

primitives.name: Large deviation exponent in dual form: the divergence exponent equals a maximum over exponential tilts (Chernoff form)
primitives.verbatim_quote: This latter form is the one usually found in textbooks
primitives.latex: \lim_{n\to\infty} -\frac{1}{n} \log \mathrm{Prob}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i) > \alpha\right) = \max_{t \ge 0} \left[ -\log \sum_a P(a) 2^{t f(a)} + t\alpha \right]

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f: a real function on the alphabet (the statistic whose mean is thresholded)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha: threshold above the true mean of f
symbol_and_unit_ledger.t: tilt parameter; the maximizing tilt defines the nearest alternative distribution Q*(a) = c* P(a) 2^{t* f(a)}

assumptions: Threshold alpha strictly between the true mean and max f
The unconstrained maximizer has t* > 0 in this regime
primitives.breakdown_regime: If alpha is at or below the true mean the exponent is 0; the dual form hides the primal geometry, and numerical maximization over t can be ill-conditioned for heavy statistics.

layer2.mapping: The dual form is the computable face of Sanov for mean-threshold events: the engine can price the rarity of an average exceeding a threshold by a one-dimensional maximization, and the maximizing tilt exhibits the least unlikely way the event happens, which is itself an interpretable scenario.
layer2.telemetry: Sample means of bounded per-event statistics; threshold exceedance queries.

primitives.name: Stein's lemma and optimal divergence tests: best type 2 error exponent is D(P1||P2); divergence-threshold tests are asymptotically optimal against all alternatives
primitives.verbatim_quote: Hence, the tests in Theorem 2.3 are asymptotically optimal against all alternatives P2 ∈ Π.
primitives.latex: \frac{1}{n} \log P_2^n(A^n - C_n) \to -D(\Pi\|P_2), \qquad C_n = \left\{ x_1^n : \inf_{P \in \Pi} D(\hat P_{x_1^n}\|P) \ge \delta_n \right\}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C_n: critical region of the test at sample size n
symbol_and_unit_ledger.delta_n: |A| log n / n, a vanishing threshold
symbol_and_unit_ledger.type 1 / type 2 error: rejecting a true null / accepting a false one

assumptions: Null set Pi closed, so D(Pi||P2) > 0 for alternatives off Pi
Tests are nonrandomized; optimality is asymptotic in exponent
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fixed sample size performance is not governed by the exponent alone; alternatives on the boundary of the null set may not have vanishing type 2 error.

layer2.mapping: Stein sets the engine's discrimination budget: distinguishing two candidate generators of categorical data costs samples in inverse proportion to their divergence, and the divergence-to-null statistic is the optimal test statistic, so model comparison modules should report exactly that quantity.
layer2.telemetry: Paired candidate distributions; samples scored by divergence to each candidate null set.

primitives.name: Sequential tests and Wald's identity: expected sample size multiplies the per-sample divergence; the SPRT attains both best exponents simultaneously
primitives.verbatim_quote: In this sense, sequential tests are not superior to tests with constant sample size.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.N: stopping time of the sequential test (random sample size)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.E_1(N): average sample size when P1 is true
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha, beta: type 1 and type 2 error probabilities of the sequential test

assumptions: I.i.d. observations; stopping set G prefix-free so N is well defined
Finite expected sample size for Wald's identity
primitives.breakdown_regime: Sequential tests cannot beat the fixed-sample exponent per expected observation; their advantage is attaining both error exponents at once, and exact likelihood-ratio constancy on the decision sets is generally unattainable, only approached.

layer2.mapping: Wald's identity is the engine's stopping economics: evidence accrues at D bits per observation, so any sequential monitoring rule can budget expected time-to-decision as target exponent divided by per-step divergence, and the SPRT thresholds are the optimal stopping shape.
layer2.telemetry: Streaming observations with running log-likelihood ratios; decision thresholds on accumulated evidence.

primitives.name: I-projection: the distribution in a closed convex set minimizing D(P||Q); divergence read as squared Euclidean distance
primitives.verbatim_quote: Information divergence of probability distributions can be interpreted as a (nonsymmetric) analogue of squared Euclidean distance.
primitives.latex: P^* = \arg\min_{P \in \Pi} D(P\|Q), \qquad D(P^*\|Q) = \min_{P \in \Pi} D(P\|Q)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Pi: a nonempty closed convex set of distributions
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P*: the I-projection of Q onto Pi, exists and is unique by strict convexity of D in its first argument

assumptions: Q(a) > 0 for all a
Pi closed and convex
primitives.breakdown_regime: The analogy is one-sided: D is not symmetric, so projecting Q onto Pi and projecting onto Q are different operations (the second is the reverse I-projection of Section 3).

layer2.mapping: I-projection is the engine's belief-revision operator: given a base projection Q and a convex set of trusted constraints, the projected distribution is the unique closest belief satisfying them, which is the principled way to impose new information without inventing any beyond the constraints.
layer2.telemetry: Base predictive distributions; constraint sets from trusted marginal or moment information.

primitives.name: Pythagorean inequality for I-projection onto a convex set, with full support of the projection
primitives.verbatim_quote: With this interpretation, several results in this Section are intuitive “information geometric” counterparts of standard results in Euclidean geometry, such as the inequality in Theorem 3.1 and the identity in Theorem 3.2.
primitives.latex: D(P\|Q) \ge D(P\|P^*) + D(P^*\|Q), \qquad \forall P \in \Pi, \quad S(P^*) = S(\Pi)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.S(P): support of P, the set of symbols with positive probability
symbol_and_unit_ledger.S(Pi): the largest support among members of Pi

assumptions: Pi closed and convex, Q strictly positive
The inequality for a candidate P* and all P in Pi is also sufficient for P* to be the projection
primitives.breakdown_regime: Only an inequality for general convex sets; equality needs the linear-family structure of Theorem 3.2.

layer2.mapping: The inequality is a free audit for any fusion step: total divergence from base to any feasible belief is at least the divergence spent reaching the projection plus the remainder, so an engine module can certify that a constraint-imposition step moved beliefs by no more than the information the constraints carry.
layer2.telemetry: Divergences before and after constraint imposition; supports of feasible distributions.

primitives.name: Linear families (moment constraints, closed) and exponential families (log-linear tilts) are dual parametrizations meeting at the I-projection
primitives.verbatim_quote: Linear families are closed sets of distributions, exponential families are not.
primitives.latex: L = \left\{ P : \sum_a P(a) f_i(a) = \alpha_i, \ 1 \le i \le k \right\}, \qquad E = \left\{ P(a) = c\, Q(a) \exp\Big( \sum_{i=1}^k \theta_i f_i(a) \Big) \right\}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_i: given real functions on A (sufficient statistics)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha_i: prescribed moment values defining the linear family
symbol_and_unit_ledger.theta_i: natural parameters of the exponential family
symbol_and_unit_ledger.c: normalizing constant, inverse sum of Q(a) exp(sum theta_i f_i(a))

assumptions: Same functions f_1..f_k define both families
Nonempty linear family; S(Q) = A
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exponential families are not closed: their closure adds boundary distributions supported on subsets (the form (3.3) of Remark 3.1), and MLEs can escape to that boundary.

layer2.mapping: This duality is the engine's two views of every parametric component: a model can be specified by the moments it must match (linear view, auditable against data) or by its tilt parameters (exponential view, fittable), and the tutorial guarantees they describe the same object at the projection.
layer2.telemetry: Moment vectors of samples; natural parameters of fitted tilts; constraint lists per model component.

primitives.name: Pythagorean identity: for a linear family the inequality becomes equality, and L intersect cl(E) is the single projection point
primitives.verbatim_quote: This proves that P ∗ satisfies the Pythagorean identity.
primitives.latex: D(P\|Q) = D(P\|P^*) + D(P^*\|Q), \qquad \forall P \in L, \quad L \cap \mathrm{cl}(E_Q) = \{P^*\}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E_Q: exponential family through Q with the same statistics
symbol_and_unit_ledger.cl(E_Q): closure of the exponential family, needed when S(L) is a proper subset of A

assumptions: Linear and exponential families defined by the same f_i
If S(L) = A then P* lies in E itself, not only its closure
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails for nonlinear constraint sets; when S(L) is smaller than A the projection sits in the closure, which is the mechanism behind nonexistent MLEs in Theorem 3.3.

layer2.mapping: The identity gives the engine an exact divergence ledger for moment matching: the cost of moving from base Q to any moment-feasible P splits into the unavoidable cost of reaching the projection plus the residual, so fitted and unfitted components of a discrepancy can be reported separately.
layer2.telemetry: Moment constraints and fitted exponential tilts; divergence budgets per constraint set.

primitives.name: Maximum likelihood is a reverse I-projection; for exponential families the MLE is the I-projection of Q onto the linear family matching the sample moments, when it exists
primitives.verbatim_quote: In the case when Π is an exponential family, the MLE equals a proper I-projection
primitives.latex: \hat P_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \arg\min_{P \in \Pi} D(\hat P\|P); \qquad \text{for } \Pi = E: \ \hat P_{\mathrm{MLE}} = P^* = \arg\min_{P \in L} D(P\|Q), \ L = \left\{ P : \sum_a P(a) f_i(a) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^n f_i(x_j) \right\}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L: linear family fixing the sample moments of the sufficient statistics
symbol_and_unit_ledger.S(L) = A: existence condition: the MLE exists in E iff the moment-matching family has full support

assumptions: Feasible set is an exponential family through a strictly positive Q
Sample arbitrary; P-hat automatically lies in L
primitives.breakdown_regime: If S(L) is a proper subset of A the MLE does not exist in E (only in its closure): a standing warning that some samples push fitted models to the boundary, where parameters diverge.

layer2.mapping: This collapses two engine subsystems into one: fitting an exponential-family component and projecting a base distribution onto data moments are the same computation, and the existence criterion S(L) = A is a pre-flight check that detects boundary-seeking fits before parameters blow up.
layer2.telemetry: Sample moment vectors; fitted natural parameters; support of the moment-matching family.

primitives.name: f-divergence: the convex-function generalization of divergence, containing KL, reversed KL, chi-square, Hellinger and variational distance
primitives.verbatim_quote: Let f (t) be a convex function defined for t > 0, with f (1) = 0. The f -divergence of a distribution P from Q is defined by
primitives.latex: D_f(P\|Q) = \sum_a Q(a) f\left( \frac{P(a)}{Q(a)} \right)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f: convex function on t > 0 with f(1) = 0
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f(t) = t log t: gives D(P||Q); f(t) = -log t gives D(Q||P); f(t) = (t-1)^2 gives chi-square divergence; f(t) = 1 - sqrt(t) gives Hellinger; f(t) = |t-1| gives variational distance

assumptions: Boundary conventions 0f(0/0) = 0 and 0f(a/0) = a lim_{u to infinity} f(u)/u
Strict convexity of f at 1 for D_f = 0 to force P = Q
primitives.breakdown_regime: Most f-divergences lack the projection transitivity and Pythagorean structure of KL (Lemma 4.2 discussion): the choice of f is a real modeling decision, not a cosmetic one.

layer2.mapping: The f-divergence menu lets the engine pick a discrepancy with known behavior: chi-square for quadratic, locally normal scoring, variational distance for worst-case event discrepancy, Hellinger for a bounded symmetric score, each inheriting nonnegativity and the lumping inequality from one convexity fact.
layer2.telemetry: Distribution pairs scored under alternative discrepancies for sensitivity checks.

primitives.name: Lumping (data processing) property: coarse-graining a distribution can only decrease every f-divergence
primitives.verbatim_quote: The first assertion and the lumping property obviously follow from the analogue of the log-sum inequality, (4.1).
primitives.latex: D_f(P\|Q) \ge D_f(P^B\|Q^B) \quad \text{for every partition } B \text{ of } A

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P^B: the B-lumping of P: probability of cell i is the sum of P over the block B_i
symbol_and_unit_ledger.B: a partition of the alphabet into blocks

assumptions: f convex; the underlying inequality (4.1) is the f-analogue of log-sum
Equality conditions require f strictly convex at the lumped ratio
primitives.breakdown_regime: Information destroyed by coarse-graining is unrecoverable: any downstream statistic computed from lumped data inherits the reduced divergence, which bounds every test or estimate built on it.

layer2.mapping: Lumping is the engine's aggregation law: binning outcomes, merging categories, or marginalizing a joint distribution can only shrink the divergence between model and data, so reported fit quality must always state the granularity at which it was measured.
layer2.telemetry: Partition choices for outcome spaces; marginal versus joint divergence reports.

primitives.name: Local quadratic equivalence: near Q every smooth f-divergence is f''(1)/2 times the chi-square divergence
primitives.verbatim_quote: does not remain true if Q is not fixed and the probabilities of Q(a) are not bounded away from 0.
primitives.latex: D_f(P\|Q) \sim \frac{f''(1)}{2} \chi^2(P, Q), \qquad \chi^2(P, Q) = \sum_a \frac{(P(a) - Q(a))^2}{Q(a)}, \quad P \to Q

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f''(1): curvature of f at 1; for f(t) = t log t it equals log e
symbol_and_unit_ledger.chi-square divergence: squared weighted Euclidean distance between P and Q

assumptions: f twice differentiable at 1 with f''(1) > 0
Q fixed with full support; probabilities of Q bounded away from 0
primitives.breakdown_regime: The equivalence collapses exactly where rare events matter: if some Q(a) can approach 0, different f-divergences disagree at leading order and tail behavior must be checked with the exact divergence, not the quadratic surrogate.

layer2.mapping: Locally, the engine can treat divergence geometry as Euclidean with the chi-square metric, which licenses least-squares style computations and normal approximations for small discrepancies, with an explicit tripwire: cells with tiny model probability exit the regime where the quadratic picture is valid.
layer2.telemetry: Cell-wise model probabilities and observed counts; minimum cell probability diagnostics.

primitives.name: Pythagorean chi-square decomposition (Wilks-type): total divergence splits into fit and model terms with independent chi-square limits and stated degrees of freedom
primitives.verbatim_quote: The χ2 distribution with k degrees of freedom is defined as the distribution of the sum of squares of k independent random variables having the standard normal distribution.
primitives.latex: D(\hat P_n\|Q) = D(\hat P_n\|P_n^*) + D(P_n^*\|Q), \qquad \frac{2n}{\log e} D(\hat P_n\|P_n^*) \Rightarrow \chi^2_{|A|-1-k}, \quad \frac{2n}{\log e} D(P_n^*\|Q) \Rightarrow \chi^2_k

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P_n*: I-projection of Q onto the random linear family matching the sample moments of f_1..f_k
symbol_and_unit_ledger.|A|-1-k: residual degrees of freedom after fitting

assumptions: f_0 = 1, f_1..f_k linearly independent; P-hat_n converges to Q
Asymptotic (large n) chi-square limits
primitives.breakdown_regime: The decomposition is exact for divergence but the chi-square limits are asymptotic; small samples and sparse cells break the approximation, and degrees of freedom change if further nested projections are taken (they still decompose additively).

layer2.mapping: This is the engine's goodness-of-fit gate: divergence of data from a fitted family comes with a null distribution and a degrees-of-freedom count, so a model family can be rejected at a stated level rather than by eyeballing a distance, and nested fits decompose the total misfit into attributable layers.
layer2.telemetry: Fitted versus empirical distributions; parameter counts per fitted family; sample sizes.

primitives.name: Log-linear models for contingency tables: fixing marginals defines a linear family whose dual exponential family is a product of interaction terms
primitives.verbatim_quote: The family of all distributions of the form (4.4) is called a log-linear family with interactions γ ∈ Γ.
primitives.latex: P(\omega) = c\, Q(\omega) \prod_{\gamma \in \Gamma} a_\gamma(\omega(\gamma))

symbol_and_unit_ledger.omega: a cell of the d-dimensional table (one category per feature)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.gamma: a subset of features; omega(gamma) is the marginal coordinate
symbol_and_unit_ledger.a_gamma: interaction factor depending on the cell only through its gamma-marginal
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Gamma: the family of interaction sets; hierarchical models close Gamma under subsets

assumptions: Uniform Q gives the classical log-linear model
Representation made unique by setting a_gamma = 1 when any component of omega(gamma) is 0
primitives.breakdown_regime: The parametrization is redundant without the hierarchical normalization; sparse tables (many zero cells) push fits to the closure boundary, the same MLE existence issue as Theorem 3.3.

layer2.mapping: Contingency structure is the engine's native format for categorical interactions: any joint distribution over discrete factors with specified marginals has a log-linear dual, so feature-interaction models can be specified by which marginals they must reproduce and fitted by projection rather than by ad hoc regression.
layer2.telemetry: Multi-way count tables: joint outcomes cross-classified by discrete situational factors.

primitives.name: Iterative scaling (IPF): cyclically rescaling to match one prescribed marginal at a time converges to the I-projection onto all of them
primitives.verbatim_quote: This applies, in particular, to I-projections to families defined by prescribed marginals, required in the analysis of contingency tables
primitives.latex: P^{(n)}(\omega) = P^{(n-1)}(\omega) \frac{\bar P_{\gamma_n}(\omega(\gamma_n))}{P^{(n-1)}_{\gamma_n}(\omega(\gamma_n))}, \qquad P^{(0)} = Q, \quad P^{(n)} \to P^*

symbol_and_unit_ledger.gamma_n: the marginal constraint applied at step n, cycling through Gamma
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P*: I-projection of Q onto the intersection of all marginal families

assumptions: Intersection of the constraint families nonempty
Each single-marginal projection has the closed scaling form (5.1)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Convergence is to the projection only when the intersection is nonempty; with incompatible marginals the cycle has no feasible limit point in the family.

layer2.mapping: Iterative scaling is the engine's workhorse solver for marginal fusion: each trusted marginal signal is imposed by an exact multiplicative rescale, the cycle provably converges to the unique least-committal joint distribution matching all of them, and the proof (a telescoping Pythagorean sum) doubles as a convergence certificate.
layer2.telemetry: Target marginal distributions per factor subset; current joint distribution iterates.

primitives.name: Generalized iterative scaling (SMART): simultaneous weighted geometric-mean updates fit I-projections to general linear families and MLEs in exponential families
primitives.verbatim_quote: Intuitively, in generalized iterative scaling the values bn (a) are updated using all constraints in each step, via multiplications by weighted geometric means of the analogues αi /βn,i of the ratios in (5.1) that have been used in standard iterative scaling, taking one constraint into account in each step.
primitives.latex: b_{n+1}(a) = b_n(a) \prod_{i=1}^k \left( \frac{\alpha_i}{\beta_{n,i}} \right)^{f_i(a)}, \qquad \beta_{n,i} = \sum_{a} b_n(a) f_i(a), \quad b_n(a) \to P^*(a)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_i >= 0 with sum_i f_i(a) = 1: normalization (5.3), achievable from arbitrary statistics by affine reparametrization plus one slack function

reasoning_traces.think: This tutorial is built around a single object, the information divergence D(P||Q), and a single claim: that most of classical statistics becomes clearer, and several of its algorithms become inevitable, once divergence is treated as a squared distance and statistical problems are treated as geometry in the space of distributions. The first movement is definitional. Entropy, conditional entropy, mutual information and divergence are introduced on a finite alphabet, with the log-sum inequality supplying nonnegativity and the Kraft inequality tying probability to code length, so that from the very start a distribution is simultaneously a belief state and a compression scheme, and the ideal code length of an outcome is minus its log probability. The second movement is combinatorial. The method of types turns multinomial probability into counting: there are only polynomially many empirical distributions of length n, each type class has size about 2^{nH}, and each carries probability about 2^{-nD} under a candidate law. Sanov's theorem and Stein's lemma are then nearly corollaries: the probability of a rare empirical pattern, and the best achievable error exponent of a test, both equal the divergence from the assumed truth to the nearest distribution in the offending set, so error exponents are distances and hypothesis testing is nearest-point geometry. The third movement is the geometry proper. The I-projection of a reference distribution onto a closed convex set satisfies a Pythagorean inequality, and onto a linear family, defined by moment constraints, a Pythagorean identity; linear families and exponential families are dual descriptions of one object, and maximum likelihood in an exponential family is exactly the projection, with the sample moments supplying the constraint values and with a sharp existence criterion in terms of support. The fourth movement turns geometry into algorithms. Projections onto single marginal constraints are simple rescalings, so cyclic projection yields iterative scaling for contingency tables; the Pythagorean identity generalizes to three-points and four-points properties that make alternating divergence minimization converge between arbitrary convex sets, and the EM algorithm falls out as the special case where one of the sets is defined by the observed marginals of incomplete data, complete with its local optimum warning outside convex problems. The fifth movement changes the question from estimating one distribution to coding for a whole class of processes. Redundancy, the excess of a code's length over the ideal minus log P, becomes the currency of model uncertainty: the normalized maximum likelihood distribution is exactly minimax for worst case redundancy, the Krichevsky-Trofimov add one half rule is revealed as a Dirichlet mixture with the Jeffreys prior, and the minimax expected redundancy of a parametric class equals a channel capacity, the I-radius of the class, which estimation based lower bounds pin at (k/2) log n for a k parameter class. The final movement spends that currency on model selection. The minimum description length principle chooses the model minimizing total description length, the model coded plus the data coded under it; with mixture or normalized maximum likelihood codes this is penalized likelihood with an exact, computable penalty whose asymptotic form is the BIC term, and consistency theorems show the true model is recovered eventually almost surely when candidates are mutually singular, while the authors' own counterexample shows the naive version of that claim fails for unbounded model lists with cheap model codes. For a reasoning engine the transferable payload is fourfold. First, divergence is a universal comparison geometry: any two belief states, forecasts, or signal summaries can be scored in bits and their disagreement decomposed along projections. Second, constraint fusion is projection: imposing trusted moment or marginal constraints on a base distribution by I-projection, computed by iterative scaling, is the principled merge that adds no information beyond the constraints. Third, complexity has a proven price list: each fitted parameter costs about half a log n bits of redundancy, so model classes can be taxed exactly rather than by taste, and the tax is attained by named mixture codes. Fourth, evidence is governed by nearest alternatives: the probability that data mislead is set by the divergence to the closest distribution that would produce them, which is the correct way to size confidence. The limits are stated just as plainly. Everything is finite alphabet, and continuous models need the general theory the authors deliberately set aside. Exponents are asymptotic and can mislead at small samples. Strong universality is impossible over the ergodic class. Alternating algorithms stall at local optima in nonconvex problems. And MDL, deployed carelessly over unbounded lists, can select infinite complexity on pure noise. Inside those limits, the tutorial is a complete operating system for turning data into beliefs: count types, project onto constraints, price parameters, and let divergences, not intuitions, set the error bars. One more strand deserves emphasis, because it is where the book stops being a survey and becomes a design manual. The algorithmic results are not a miscellany: iterative scaling, generalized iterative scaling, alternating minimization and EM are one algorithm viewed at four levels of generality, each justified by the same Pythagorean bookkeeping, so an implementer who understands the projection theorem understands why all four converge and exactly when each can fail. Likewise the coding results are one theorem viewed from three sides: the normalized maximum likelihood distribution is the minimax answer for worst case redundancy, the mixture construction is the practical answer for expected redundancy, and the capacity identity is the information theoretic answer explaining why both prices coincide at (k/2) log n. A reader who internalizes that unity can move between estimation, compression and model selection without changing tools, which is precisely the fluency a reasoning engine needs when the same evidence must be scored, fused and taxed inside a single pipeline.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from Boltzmann's combinatorial entropy through Shannon's 1948 coding theorems and the Kullback and Leibler divergence of 1951, Wald's sequential analysis, and Sanov's 1957 large deviation theorem, all of which already used divergence as the exponent of error. Kullback proposed divergence minimization as an inference principle in 1959; Cencov and Amari later uncovered the differential geometry underneath it, and Csiszar's 1975 I-divergence geometry paper supplied the projection theorems this tutorial teaches. The algorithmic line runs from Kruithof's 1937 scaling through Darroch and Ratcliff's generalized iterative scaling to the Dempster, Laird and Rubin EM algorithm of 1977. The coding line runs from Fitingof and Davisson through Krichevsky and Trofimov and Shtarkov's normalized maximum likelihood to Rissanen's MDL principle and Schwarz's BIC, closing with Barron's redundancy theory and the authors' own work on BIC consistency for Markov order estimation.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors write for a reader who knows basic probability and distrusts black boxes: every theorem is proved, usually by elementary counting, and every abstraction is immediately cashed out as a statistical procedure. Their model of the domain is that statistics and compression are one subject seen from two sides, so a good estimator should induce a good code and a good code should reveal the model that generated the data. They deliberately restrict attention to finite alphabets, trading generality for a setting where combinatorics replaces analysis and the geometry stays visible. Their recurring rhetorical move is Euclidean analogy: divergence is introduced as a squared distance analogue, and projections, Pythagoras, radius and centroid follow, with the reader expected to import geometric intuition wholesale and then note precisely where the analogy bends, since divergence is not symmetric and satisfies no triangle inequality.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results act as vetoes on other layers of any system built from this material. The singularity phenomenon behind Theorems 8.1 and 8.3 vetoes any pipeline whose model assigns probability zero to events the truth can produce: redundancy then grows without bound and no amount of data repairs a support error, so support coverage must be audited before fitting begins. The absence of strongly universal codes for the ergodic class vetoes any claim that one fixed model class performs uniformly well over all stationary sources; adaptivity or explicit mixtures are mandatory, not optional. The MDL counterexample vetoes naive consistency claims for unbounded model lists with slowly growing model codes: selection can diverge to infinite order on the simplest true model unless an order bound or a full strength penalty is imposed. Finally, the chi-square theory vetoes fixed universal thresholds for goodness of fit, because the same divergence statistic carries different null distributions depending on how many parameters were fitted, so every divergence passed upward must travel with its degrees of freedom.

universal_lens: Read as a general template, the tutorial says: pick a divergence and you have picked a geometry; pick a geometry and estimation becomes projection, algorithms become alternating projection, and model choice becomes accounting. Any domain whose states are distributions over finitely many outcomes, whose constraints arrive as moments or marginals, and whose models arrive as nested families can run the same operating system: compare states by divergence, fuse constraints by projection, tax each parameter at half a log of the sample size, and judge evidence by the distance to the nearest alternative that would explain the data. The specific content is information theory; the reusable form is a discipline for turning counting into inference without ever leaving the geometry that makes the answers checkable.
gsi_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Institute this tutorial is a curriculum spine for evidence theory. It supplies the cleanest available route from counting (types) to large deviations (Sanov), to testing exponents (Stein), to projection based belief revision, to universal coding and MDL, with each step proved by elementary tools. It fixes the vocabulary the institute teaches for talking about sample evidence: exponents are divergences, fitted parameters cost half a log n bits, and goodness of fit decomposes by projection with chi-square limits and stated degrees of freedom. It also supplies the cautionary exhibits for the syllabus: the MDL consistency counterexample, the failure of strong universality over ergodic processes, and the breakdown of f-divergence equivalence when small model probabilities are not bounded away from zero.
gse_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Edge engine this tutorial contributes machinery, not picks. Divergence is the scoring geometry for comparing a projected distribution over game outcomes with the realized empirical distribution, and its Pythagorean decomposition separates misfit caused by wrong marginals from misfit inside the model family. I-projection is the fusion operator: a base projection is adjusted to match trusted marginal signals such as usage shares, availability rates and situational frequencies by iterative scaling, which is exactly the constraint structure of contingency tables. Redundancy supplies the complexity tax for every fitted component, (k/2) log n per parameter block, and the normalized maximum likelihood and Dirichlet mixture constructions give concrete priors, add one half smoothing, for sparse categorical estimates. EM covers latent state estimation from incomplete observations, with the tutorial's local optimum warning attached.
